utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. If there are no procedural matters or other issues to be raised, the witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; morning to the Defence; good morning, everyone. Just a quick update on Dr. Haglund's situation while the witness is being brought in. We've explored with him the possibility, putting all the technical practicality issues aside, as to whether he could be available for a videolink testimony at the end of next week. He is willing, but his medical situation is such that if his heart rate elevates at any particular time, his doctor will order him to the hospital. Given that contingency alone, I think, given all the mechanics required to get the videolink set up, we'll just reschedule and I'll ask the Court some additional questions regarding that at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that update.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. And Mr. Thayer has some more questions during his redirect. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the Honourable Presiding Judge's last question to you at the very end of yesterday's session went a long way to clarifying matters. At page 84 of yesterday's transcript, you answered: "All of the brigades were based on geographical distribution. One area had one brigade, another area had another, the third had its own. So the brigades were comprised of the local population, and inside each brigade two or three people were selected to co-ordinate. We, however, were in the town itself and we were a link between the brigade military policemen and the command." Do you recall that testimony from yesterday? I know it was sort of an eventful afternoon for you, I just want to make sure you recall that, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when in your witness statement, for example, and this is at page 2, where you say that you didn't go to the front lines but that as a military policemen you worked between the brigades, the language you used in your witness statement, is that what you meant there, that you were a link between the brigades?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is P1373.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again building on your answer to the Honourable Presiding Judge's question of yesterday, so when at page 49 of yesterday's transcript General Tolimir asked you, "Did you belong to a brigade or a staff," you answered, "I think a staff." And then on the next page you explained that it was, and I quote, "the staff of the command of the Srebrenica defence." Again, just building on your answer to the Honourable Presiding Judge's question at the end of yesterday, is that what you are referring to when you said that you were a member of a staff, this link between the brigades?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that sense, because, among other things, in one of the shifts there would be four or five young men patrolling around town, looking what is going on. If any soldiers were creating any problems, they would report to one of our superiors and they would report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your JNA training and in your experience as a military policemen in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what is the purpose of a military staff such as the one to which you belonged? What is the general purpose of a staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no training as a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I was an MP in the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And my question is simply, and again if you can answer it; if you don't think you can answer it, that's fine, but based on your training and your experience as an MP, can you tell the Trial Chamber, just generally, what is the purpose of a military staff such as the one to which you belonged when you were an MP?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army recruited into its military police people who were fit, trained - I'm talking about the former JNA - they had undergone good training, they had to have good people skills, good communication skills, establish a dialogue with another person, use the powers that the police had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you the question a different way. Can you tell the Trial Chamber in your experience what were the duties, the typical duties of a military policeman, first? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking strictly about our work. Unless we got some specific order from the police commander, the young men who would be on patrol duty would patrol around town, submit a report to the commander about what was going on on the ground, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your role during the time-period that you served as an MP, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you had those types of duties or whether you had other types of duties as a member of this staff that you've described for us.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rarely walked around town on patrol. I'll tell you first of all how it came about that this military police was formed. Armed men sometimes arrogated the right to pose as anyone and do what they like. That's how the idea occurred to someone that a military police should be formed, a military police that would have some authority and check such behaviour. That's how we operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber how, if at all, your personal duties - I'm just talking about you, sir, when you were serving as an MP in Srebrenica - how, if at all, were your duties different from the duties of the MPs who you told us were assigned to the various brigades in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, MPs attached to brigades were subordinated exclusively to their brigade commanders or company commanders and could receive orders only from them. We, on the other hand, were stationed in the town itself, and that's where we did whatever needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us that there was a military police commander and that his name, if I've got it correctly, was Sakib Krdzic, or something to that effect, and he lived in the same building, upstairs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krdzic, that's right. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Krdzic have a rank of any kind that you recall?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an active-duty policeman, I really don't know if he had a rank. See one thing, before the arrival of the UNPROFOR, there were no ranks in Srebrenica, there was nothing. It was only after we established some sort of communication with Tuzla and Sarajevo that they started assigning ranks to commanding officers. I really don't know who had which rank, and you have to believe me if I say that I wasn't really interested in these things. And one more thing: No one in Srebrenica had rank or rank insignia and I never saw any rank insignia on ABiH army officers until I arrived in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just told us that Mr. Krdzic was an active-duty policeman. Do you know whether he was a professional military officer or had any military experience beyond, for example, his mandatory JNA training?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And to whom did Mr. Krdzic report? Who was his direct superior officer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but probably someone in the top command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "top command," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean all the brigades, when they sat down together, he probably gave them a report or a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And was it your understanding that -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one more thing: I know that all brigade commanders were able to give orders to Sakib, what he should do. They were able to give him orders what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, that was my next question for you, and I'll ask it again just to make sure we've got it clear. In the military hierarchy of command, was the staff to which you belonged superior to, subordinate to, or at an equal level with the brigades, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was subordinate to brigades. First of all, because there were very few people, and second, we were like a service catering to all brigades. So all brigade commanders were able to give orders to Sakib Krdzic and he passed those orders down the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, may I put one additional question. Sir, when you say "all brigade commanders were able to give orders," do you mean the commanders of the different regional brigades and the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one final question on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I take it that there was a brigade whose area of responsibility included the town of Srebrenica in which your office was located?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not strictly for Srebrenica, but there was one brigade made up of people from the peripheral areas, such as Konjevic Polje, Kamenica. Those that fell in 1993. Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica. These people who had fled these parts and moved to Srebrenica, they formed one brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask it a different way. I'm just focusing on, for example, down-town, the centre of the town of Srebrenica. I take it that there was some formation, be it a brigade, a battalion, some military formation, whose responsibility it was to protect or defend that area of responsibility, that geographical circumference of that part of the town or, if it was covered by various units, so be it let us know, but can you tell us whether you were aware that there was a unit or units whose area of responsibility included that down-town area where you had your office?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact only lines around Srebrenica were defended. In the town itself there was neither military activity nor any other similar activity in the town itself, but people lived in the town and they knew exactly what their roster was and when they should go to the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Tolimir asked you, and this was at page 50 of yesterday's transcript, where the staff's location, and that would be the staff of the command of the Srebrenica defence that you spoke about, where that location was in 1992 and 1993, and you answered "at the Territorial Defence staff"; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's the same building that used to house the Territorial Defence staff inside the town and that's where the command was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you told us that Naser Oric didn't spend a whole lot of time there because he was in the field. I just want to follow-up on a question that the Honourable Presiding Judge asked you about that building itself. You said it used to be the former Territorial Defence quarters. Can you tell us what kind of building it was? Was it an apartment building, a store, a warehouse? Did it have some recognisable peacetime function? You know, for example, there were certain things in the PTT building, we've heard testimony that there was a small communications room in the PTT building. The Judges have been to Srebrenica. If this was a non-descript building, just tell us, but if there's some other way to describe this building other than the former TO building, just let us know just so we can have an idea of what this building actually was.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's office space with offices, and the TO operated until the very beginning of the war, until just before the war. Mr. Tolimir can probably explain it to you better. It was a service of the Yugoslav People's Army. People just moved into these offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And as the TO offices, that would have been sufficient in itself so that everybody would recognise it as such; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone who lived in Srebrenica I believed knew that staff and knew where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to give us a little bit of background, can you just very briefly explain to us what the Territorial Defence, which we are abbreviating as TO, meant? What was it? You mentioned it a few times, we've heard the abbreviation TO, Territorial Defence, thrown about a little bit; can you just tell us what its function was, what its purpose was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence staff there were reserve military officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army. Their task was to make a list of all military-age able-bodied men to make and issue wartime assignments to everyone so that manpower can be mobilised as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you further clarified yesterday, and this was at page 52, that your office, where you spent your time, was in the old police building which was about a kilometre and a half from the old TO office building. Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit more about where this old police building was located in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The building of the old police station was located -- I don't know if you have a plan of Srebrenica, it's when you go from the post office halfway towards the staff. It was a little bit closer to the staff than to the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how close was it, for example, to the UN compound in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A kilometre and a half, maybe two.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, while I was there, there was no UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "when I was there" what do you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean before the UNPROFOR arrived, the police operated. With the arrival of the UNPROFOR, that unit was disbanded, no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, yesterday General Tolimir told you that the Republika Srpska Assembly had made the Ekavian dialect mandatory. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the Ekavian dialect is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ekavian dialect is a way of pronouncing words prevalent in Serbia. For instance, in Bosnia we would say, for the word "children,"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "djeca."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as a Bosniak born and raised in Eastern Bosnia, do you consider Ekavian your native dialect?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Serbs and Muslims in Srebrenica spoke the Ijekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the words sound similar, but are they different dialects, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir also told you that the Republika Srpska Assembly made the Cyrillic alphabet mandatory. You testified that you were taught both Latinic and Cyrillic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, in Eastern Bosnia did the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Serb communities prefer one alphabet over the other or traditionally use one over the other?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In school we would learn what was then called the Serbo-Croat language, writing in one script for seven days and then the next seven days the other script, but we learned the Roman script more than the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "we," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who lived in Srebrenica. They made it mandatory. It was an Assembly decision to make it mandatory because the Cyrillic script had not been mandatory before that time. That's why they introduced that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what alphabet or script did you use day in and day out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Roman script and the Ijekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the other Bosnian Muslims of your community, sir; what script did they use and what dialect did they speak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same. They all used the Roman script and the Ijekavian dialect. Only those children who attended high school in Serbia, they signed themselves in Cyrillic letters for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So tell us, sir, what did these laws that General Tolimir cited tell you, as a non-Serb, about how you, as a non-Serb, could expect to be treated if you found yourself living under Republika Srpska authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone and I would like to have these proceedings concluded by God's will and not my own. I'd like to greet the witness. Thank you for the floor. This calls for speculation. I quoted the law to the witness whereas Mr. Thayer is asking for speculation. He should adjust his questions to the procedure, having in mind the regulation of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a perfectly fair question that follows directly on General Tolimir's questions that raised these specific issues. General Tolimir raised the issue of these laws and I'm simply asking this witness, who lived through this period, grew up within his community, how these laws that General Tolimir spoke about -- what they tell him, what they tell him based on his experience, Mr. President, about how he could expect to be treated. What does a law like that tell him based on his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And with this explanation, it is not beyond the scope of re-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand it. As long as my human rights, that is the right to express myself and my right to speech, are not in danger, I will feel on my own in Srebrenica and I will reside there. I have a house there, I frequently visit the area. I know that the overall situation is somewhat discriminatory, but since I can write in that script, I will use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In Republika Srpska the right of Muslims to use their dialect and script is not denied. The witness, furthermore, is speaking in Croatian, which is also not prohibited, so I believe this is all speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a statement, but the Prosecution is examining the witness. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness wants to add something to your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir probably doesn't know, but there is no Bosnian language in Srebrenica. It is not denied, though, but the children are still following the Belgrade curriculum and not the curriculum of either the RS or Sarajevo, as it should be. And this is the latest information from Srebrenica. That is precisely why my children do not attend school in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Question for clarification, General Tolimir said that you speak Croatian. Do you confirm this? Is that what you speak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croat language had been used in the former Yugoslavia. It is for that reason that we all understand each other, the Croats, Serbs, and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that. But what language are you speaking right now to us?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it to be the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But you also said that today in the curriculum -- in Srebrenica it's the Belgrade curriculum that is taught, is that what you said? And this is the reason why you do not send your children to school in Srebrenica; is that true?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may just follow up on the question from Honourable Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Again, which dialect are you speaking?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ijekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you again something about the language you use. We know about the Serbo-Croatian language, but you told us there is no specific Bosnian language. Serbo-Croatian language is composed of two quite similar but distinct languages, Serbian and Croatian. What is your language you are using?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the former Yugoslavia fell apart, in Croatia, Serbia, and Bosnia, the people assumed the right to speak the way they wanted to. I'll take the example of the word "coffee." In Serbia, it is "kava," in Bosnia it is "kahva," and in Croatia it is "kafa." The meaning is the same but there are some changes in the word itself. That's why I believe Bosnian is separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And which language are you using? I'm only speaking about your personal experience.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to insist on this to make sure that I really understand what we are talking about. You said that you speak Bosnian, the Bosnian language. To one of the questions put to you by Mr. Thayer, you said that it was the Ijekavian dialect. Now, as far as the Defence is concerned, and General Tolimir, you are speaking Croatian, but he speaks Serbian, so could you tell me exactly whether you deny what General Tolimir said and that you are not speaking Croatian? So please confirm that you are speaking Bosnian but in the Ijekavian dialect. Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the language of my state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination. You are now free to return to your normal activities and your usual life. The Chamber would like to thank you that you came here to The Hague and to assist us in finding the truth. Thank you very much again. And the court usher will assist you leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to thank you for enabling me to testify in an orderly fashion, that the truth come out and that it is only the truth that is seriously considered before this Tribunal and that all those who deserve to be sanctioned be indeed punished. I apologise if I occasionally overreacted but that was for emotional reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for these words, and good-bye again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well, good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, is the next witness prepared and ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He is waiting in the wings, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I was told that there's no witness in the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The plan and instructions we had in place last night were that he were to be brought down at 0900, so there obviously was something not communicated or lost somewhere. It may be just a five-minute recess, or if we can just stand by and we don't need to go anywhere, just give us a minute, I can run out and see what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the court usher has left the courtroom to find out what is happening. The Court Officer is calling. We should just wait here for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that the witness was waiting in a wrong waiting room but he will be brought to the courtroom immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Mr. President, we could use this time to discuss the scheduling issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The -- as I understood from, I think, what Mr. McCloskey had mentioned, there was some discussion that the Chamber might begin sitting on Monday, 17 January in light of the Orthodox holiday, thereby extending the recess, I think, a week. I notice that on the court calendar had been issued we are scheduled to sit on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. It was not conveyed in a proper way to those who are responsible for the court calendar. That was corrected yesterday and you will see on the next update that we are not sitting in the week commencing on the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. That's good to know, Mr. President. What I think -- I see the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think what we'll try to do, then, is schedule Dr. Haglund perhaps to be the first witness after the recess. We'll explore that, but that may work out the best, give him sufficient time, but I still think it will probably be videolink testimony, just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Good morning. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be examined today here in the trial, and the first putting questions to you is Mr. Thayer of the Prosecution. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I forgot to advise the Court that, in line with the prior trial and the status of the witness, a caution is in order, I think, as just a matter of routine for this witness, pursuant to Rule 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: According to this information and advice, I would like to give some information for the witness. Sir, it's not the first time that you are testifying here in the Tribunal, but I have to give you an information and a kind of warning. Our Rules of Procedure and Evidence have a Rule 90, and in paragraph (E) of this rule, there is written the following, and I quote: "The witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We haven't properly met since June of 2007. I'm sorry I couldn't properly introduce myself to you on Sunday, owing to my illness, but I'll do so now, and good morning to you again. Could you state your name, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Dobrisav Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall testifying in this courtroom for just over two days on the 19th and 20th of June, 2007, in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Borovcanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, he was one of the seven accused, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to listen to that testimony this past Sunday?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest that that recording accurately reflects what you said during your testimony in the prior case?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest that if you were asked the same questions again today that you were asked back in 2007, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I would definitely provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time the Prosecution would tender P01263 and 1264, the under seal and public versions of the witness's prior testimony in the Popovic matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These exhibits will be received. The exhibit P1263 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at this time, Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender associated exhibits P1265 to 1277, and I'll reserve discussion and usage on the remaining exhibits for a little while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These documents will be received. Are they all public? I think so, yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the prior trial, I'm sure you recall being shown a number of photographs and video-clips from footage that was taken in Potocari and along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. There were a couple of specific photographs that were shown to you in the prior trial that, through administrative error, didn't make it into the record yet in this case, so what I'd like to do is show you some additional photos. I don't think they will be any surprise to you, but I want to show you some photos and just see if you can identify the people in them. You were actually, I can tell you, shown these photos, and I'll cite to you what you said to them before, but we just need to do it in front of this Trial Chamber and it shouldn't take too much time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, are you going to read a witness summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I knew there was something I forgot, Mr. President. It seemed we were moving a little too quickly. Thank you for reminding me, I do have a summary to read. I'll do that now. The witness was born in Zalazje, Srebrenica municipality, and was raised in Srebrenica. In the spring of 1992 he joined a unit called the Srebrenica Guard which consisted of about 30 soldiers who were refugees from Srebrenica. The Srebrenica Guard was dismantled in mid-1992 and became part of the Bratunac Brigade's 3rd Battalion. In March of 1993, he transferred from the VRS to the MUP. After undergoing a police training course in Jahorina, he was assigned to the police station in Bratunac where he worked as a beat police officer. At the time, Luka Bogdanovic was the police station chief, Ljubisa Borovcanin was the police station commander. Sometime in late 1993 or early 1994, Borovcanin left to take up a new function in the Special Police. The witness also described his duties as a member of the 1st Company of the Zvornik PJP. The 1st Company was comprised of policemen from the Zvornik, Milici, Vlasenica, Sekovici, Bratunac, and Skelani police stations. Radomir Pantic was the commander of the 1st Company, which was divided into three platoons. The witness's platoon was commanded by Dusan Micic. The witness received an order on 11 July 1995 to report to the police station with all his combat equipment and to wait for the rest of the 1st Company. He waited there for awhile, then left and returned the following morning, 12 July. He joined the 1st Company at Yellow Bridge where they waited until a dead Bratunac Brigade de-miner was taken away. They then deployed in a firing line and moved towards Potocari. Their task was to search the terrain, take the right-hand side of the hill, and go all the way down to Potocari to look for any remaining Muslim soldiers. At that time they had heard that the VRS had taken Srebrenica and that there were civilians in Potocari. Pantic and Micic were with them and communicated by Motorola radio. There were also Special Police Brigade and VRS units advancing with them. They covered the area on the right-hand side of the road leading to Srebrenica, and since they encountered no one, they descended from the hills to the road after an hour or two. Before they reached the part of the road which the UN had cordoned off with yellow tape, they encountered a group of civilians crossing the road. When he reached the cordoned off area, the witness saw VRS and Special Police Brigade soldiers already there, along with UNPROFOR members. His unit stayed there for awhile until General Mladic arrived, after which the witness took up a position in an orchard near the zinc factory for an hour or two. From his position, he saw two or three buses and trucks arrive, make a U-turn, and park, waiting to board civilians. He did not see any Muslim men being separated or detained, nor did he see anyone board the buses. Before the civilians began boarding the buses, his unit received an order to return to Bratunac, so their bus arrived and took them back to Bratunac where they awaited further orders for a while. They then received orders to board the bus, which headed towards Zvornik and stopped at Sandici in the early evening. They deployed along the road and were told to secure it. Also deployed on the road were a Praga, a three-barrelled combat vehicle, and a tank. At approximately 0400 or 0500 hours on 13 July, the witness was awakened by an explosion and shooting. Three 1st Company officers were wounded and one, Zeljko Ninkovic, a police officer from the Bratunac police station, was killed. After this incident, the witness moved up the road and took cover in a destroyed house. While there, he saw people coming out of the woods, passing the house, and sitting down in a meadow across the road. Sometime that morning he returned to Bratunac to organise the funeral for Ninkovic. The witness was also shown numerous photo stills from the Srebrenica trial video and identified various soldiers he recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me just follow up with a couple of questions and then we'll deal with some of these photographs. The Trial Chamber has heard a little bit of testimony about these units that we referred to as PJP units. The Trial Chamber has heard that they are comprised of policemen from various police stations. Now, sir, normally in the MUP what colour uniform does a civilian police officer wear? And I'm talking about July of 1995, for example.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the normal activities the police wore camouflage blue uniforms, and when we went into combat, we would put on green camouflage, like the army, similar to the military camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And was every normal beat police officer also a member of a PJP unit, or only some?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: All of us. We were distributed, I think, into six companies, and I belonged to the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you describe that there were three platoons in the 1st Company of the Zvornik PJP. Do you recall which platoon number you were in? If you don't, that's okay, just wondering if you recall whether it was 1, 2, or 3 platoon?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 3rd Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has heard reference to this location called Yellow Bridge, in your language Zuti Most. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where that was located in relation to the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Yellow Bridge is on the main road leading to Srebrenica from Bratunac and it's roughly on the boundary between Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities and it's about eight kilometres away from Srebrenica, heading towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how close was it to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's about three, perhaps four kilometres to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at Yellow Bridge, was there any VRS presence or check-point of any kind?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether that check-point was manned by any person in particular?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. The Yellow Bridge is the place where I turned to the right, and the check-point was a bit further ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever hear of a Bratunac Brigade soldier with a nickname Jovo who perhaps had been a Russian teacher? Does that ring any bells? If not, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I heard the name. He was called "Jovo the Russian." I think I know the man even.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you ever hear that he manned that check-point? And again, if you didn't, that's fine. Just checking what your knowledge of that check-point was.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was also a UN observation point somewhere in the vicinity of Yellow Bridge?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, not far from our own check-point at the Yellow Bridge, it was perhaps 200, 300 metres towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you two aerial photographs you marked in the last trial just to give the Trial Chamber a better overview of some of your movements during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P1276 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have an image in front of you, sir, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember making these markings on the 19th of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall what the arrow there that we can see in red moving along the road in front of the UN compound depicts?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the route along which my unit moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And then we see a small circle, if you move further right, at the intersection of that main road and perhaps a smaller path or a road that branches off to the right as you head south towards Srebrenica. Do you remember circling that area and identifying that as the position where you encountered a group of civilians who subsequently moved across the road to the UN base?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we move further to the right, there's a small X. Does that represent the orchard that you testified about where you positioned yourself for some time on that day?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we are done with this exhibit. May we see P1277 for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see here we have an aerial image of the area of Sandici. Do you remember -- if we see the marking number 1, do you remember identifying that as the small house where you were positioned for a period of time along that road next to the meadow or near the meadow at Sandici?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what you have marked on this image as number 2? Do you recall what that is there where you wrote the number 2?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a destroyed house by which civilians passed going towards the meadow which I marked with number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that that destroyed house was much larger, even though it was destroyed, than the small house which you've marked as number 1?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's certainly much bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall it being on a slight hill?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's number 2 on a small hillock.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for the clarification. And what have you marked as number 3 here, sir?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Number 3 is the meadow. When we got approval from our commander that we may go organise the funeral, on the way where I marked the meadow is where I saw people in civilian clothing, mostly men, a certain number of them. I can't say how many, I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And lastly, what is the X that you've marked on this image?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's where I was in the night when we were attacked when our colleague Mr. Ninkovic was killed, when he was just next to me, and other colleagues were wounded, and what is marked by X is the place where I was, together with Ninkovic when he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at some additional photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have P1369, please. This is the trial video stills book about which Ms. Gallagher has been testifying. Now, Mr. President, what I propose to do is show various photographs that are contained within this book. There we go, got it. That's the correct book. I just wanted to orient the Trial Chamber to the exhibit we are talking about, this book of video stills that Investigator Gallagher has been testifying about. I'm going to show the witness some photographs that are contained in this book but without the identifying information that the Trial Chamber will recall is contained in the book, so it will be just the photographs that form the basis for some of the pages in this book. So for the Trial Chamber's references, we don't need to go to these pages because I don't want to show the witness the actual pages from the book, only the photographs. Ms. Stewart will show the photographs from Sanction, but just for the Court's reference, we are looking at a photograph which is at page 45 of 65 ter 369. We can see this image bears 0216-4836.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we can see a young man in a uniform carrying what appears to be an automatic rifle, with his arm slightly raised, to the right of the image. Can you identify who that man is, sir?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record, the witness was shown this photograph at transcript page 12892 and it's identified in the prior record by that ERN that I quoted a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another image. This is from page 79 of 65 ter 1369. This is at 0216-4737 in the Popovic trial, and this is at transcript page 12895. You were shown this image, and again it's ERN 0216-4737. You testified that, "This is a colleague from Milici whose name I don't know. He belonged to the Milici police station." Do you recall saying that about this individual?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, although this image, or rather, his face here is not very clear, but I'm pretty sure it's one of the members of the police station in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear, we are referring to the man who has got an automatic rifle balanced on his shoulder, with his profile to the camera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question. You told us that this colleague was from the Milici police station. Was he at that time a normal police officer of that police station or a PJP member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of us were regular policemen in our stations and we were engaged, as required, to join the 1st Company of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you are referring to yourself and to the police officer, your colleague, depicted in this photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that applies to the two of us and all the others as well. Everyone in the 1st Company were professional policemen and we regularly responded to call-ups from the centre to join the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one last photograph. This is at page 80 of 65 ter 1369. We see here an image with the ERN 0216-4735, and again at transcript page 12895 you testified that you couldn't be 100 per cent sure but you think that this individual in the middle of the image with the white headband is somebody named -- nicknamed "Cop," that you are about 70/30 per cent sure that it was somebody that you knew as "Cop." Do you recall saying that in the prior trial, sir?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Cop was his nickname. I stand by that. I believe it's him but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I want to show you just one other document, and let's start off by showing it on e-court and see how successful we are. If we need to go to the original version, we can put it on the ELMO or I can give it to you to look at and you can also read off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P01042, please. And we'll need to go to page 27 of the original document. We don't really need the English translation right now, it won't be particularly helpful. And if we could blow it up a little bit, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Thayer, this was received under seal in the Popovic trial. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, we should probably err on the side of caution with respect to this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: However, we would like to have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Meanwhile, you were shown this document in the last trial, and for the record, that was at transcript page 12918. What it is, just to refresh your recollection, is a log-book, a patient log from the Bratunac health centre, which shows the admission of various patients in 1995. You were shown that by one of the Defence counsel in the prior trial and I just want to show it to you here. It's somewhat hard to read, but do you see the date of 13 July 1995 and a time of 0445 hours?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that corresponds to entry number 1481; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who is the individual who is listed here as the patient?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a colleague who worked with me, Zeljko Ninkovic. He got killed that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And does this time here -- or can you tell the Trial Chamber how the time that's listed here, 0445 hours, corresponds to your recollection of the timing of the events that you've told the Trial Chambers about this attack that occurred on the road where Mr. Ninkovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that's what I said, more or less, and when I see this time indication here, it's right, because we were in position, most of us were exhausted and were sleeping, and that's probably when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P010042 (sic). I think it's been -- it may have been MFI'd in connection with another witness, but just to be on the safe side I wanted to show the witness the document so that it could be properly tendered, and we'll do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, with respect to the remainder of the documents that are on the Prosecution's exhibit list, I think we can take care of those matters outside the presence of the witness, if the Chamber prefers. It's purely administrative matters. I think we can wait until the conclusion of the cross-examination to do that rather than taking up time when he is here, although I'm happy to do it, if the Court pleases, right now while we are in the tendering process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If it's not too time consuming, you should do it in the usual way with the witness. But let me ask something to the last document, P1042, which we just received under seal, does that contain many pages? Because you were referring only to page 27. Is it the whole book or only this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is a photocopy of the whole log-book. Like most of the log-books and notebooks that we come into possession of, our practice is to put the whole log-book in even though we are going to refer only to a page or two. I can tell the Trial Chamber that there are other relevant pages in this book that other witnesses unconnected to the current witness will testify about in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, did you want to get the floor? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to say that the witness testified only about Zeljko Ninkovic and not the others from the list. For the sake of the witness, given that the witness was cautioned, Mr. Thayer should limit his questions only to the extent of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that objection has no basis in fact or law. There's no reason to attach any potential exposure, criminal exposure of this witness to anything that's in that notebook. General Tolimir knows that there are other relevant pages in this book, so there's no valid reason to deny its admission on such a basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In any case, we must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00. The court usher will assist you, sir, during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we just go into private session for one more question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would withdraw its motion to tender two exhibits, P010097 (sic)and P01278 with respect to this witness because they have been superseded by 65 ter 1369, which is the video stills book that Ms. Gallagher has been testifying about. The two exhibits I just mentioned were older versions of that video stills book. Virtually all of the photographs that are contained in the older versions are contained in the version 1369, which the Trial Chamber has seen a lot of, so I thought I would just make things a little bit cleaner without loading up e-court with redundant, out-of-date exhibits which will be replaced by 1369 in any event. So we withdraw 1097 and 1278, which is 65 ter 6620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Defence take a position on that? Mr. Tolimir or Mr. Gajic? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to check these documents and we come back to that application later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. President, the Chamber will note that we have P1279 also on the list. That in the meantime, since the generation of this list, has been admitted as an exhibit through Mr. Blaszczyk and his road book testimony, so that, I think, is already an exhibit in this case. And that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Sir, we have seen some pictures where we could see some members of the PJP from the Milici police station and they were guarding prisoners. I'm thinking about page 79 taken from the 65 ter list and document 1369 presented by the Prosecutor. On this page we saw a picture of Mr. Osmanovic if I'm not mistaken about his name, and he was calling his son called Nermin. And you did recognise Milici policeman, and this policeman was carrying an automatic gun. So you did tell us that these members of the Milici police station were called in order to rally the 1st Company of the PJP unit. And I would like to ask you a question. Of course if you don't know, you don't know, it's not a problem, but I have a few questions. My first question is as follows: What was the role played by these members of the 1st Company of this PJP unit? What did they do with their prisoners? That was my first question, because we did see some members of your unit next to the prisoners and they were carrying guns, so I would like to know what was your role regarding the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not participate in that. Up until the moment when I was there, just before I left, on the left-hand side on the meadow I marked, I could see the people who had surrendered. They were secured not only by the people of my unit, but there were some other units as well. I don't know anything about their role, though. I didn't hear about that from anyone. They were probably there to prevent them from escaping, although I don't know what the exact orders may have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a second question, and of course if you know, you know; if you do not know, it's not a problem. Who gave an order to these Milici policemen for them to rally the 1st Company? Who gave that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All stations that were part of the CSB in Zvornik received dispatches. Such dispatches are used to inform the stations what members should be dedicated to the unit, and then the stations notify the individual policemen who gather at designated assembly points. In this particular case, that assembly point was in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know which authority sent these dispatches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only know it arrived from the CSB in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. Thank you. And I have another question. During the mission, your colleagues who were part of the 1st Company, were they placed under the authority of the police or of the army? Once they did take part, once they participated to the work with the prisoners, who did they report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really not familiar with the chain of command. We were subordinated to our officers first and foremost, but I don't know whether they received orders from the army or the top of the police. I know that on occasion when we were in the field we jointly worked with the army, but I don't know who was in actual command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. This is quite enough for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I have a clarification, rather, an amplification. When Mr. Thayer was summarising your evidence, what you were going to say, and correct me if I'm wrong, page 23, lines 1 to 9 of today's testimony, he stated that you were awakened by an explosion and shooting. "The 1st Company officers were wounded and one Ninkovic, a police officer from the Bratunac police station was killed." Who was shooting at you in this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The members of Muslim units, of their army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the second question is: Within the same page and line numbers, Mr. Thayer said, "While there, you saw people coming out of the woods, passing the house and sitting down in a meadow across the road." Who are these people that you saw coming down and sitting down in the meadow across the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were people from Srebrenica, Muslims. I don't know whether they were army members or civilians. There were some in uniform, though, but I don't know who belonged to what entity, but those were the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I have a question for you, sir: We have seen today a photograph where you identified yourself. We saw a soldier and you said this is -- or a policeman, and you said it would be yourself, and there were some women on the left side of this photograph. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was happening at that point in time with these women? Where did they come from? What was the reason why they were there? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we arrived from the direction of Bratunac on the right-hand side, where the electrical power-station is, a group of women and children arrived. Some women were obviously scared and crying. I spoke to them, saying that they shouldn't be afraid, that they should feel free to approach us. I asked them where they were headed to and they answered the base of the UN. One of our officers who was there, although I don't remember who exactly, told me to escort them. He -- I simply had to see them across the road, perhaps 20 or 30 metres down the road, where DutchBat members were. I escorted them to that point and they were received there when the soldiers opened the gate. They entered the base, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Tolimir has questions for you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet the witness, and I wish him a pleasant stay here and a safe return home. May God bless him. I have no questions of him since most of the questions I intended to put were put by the Bench itself. Everything is clear and hence I'm left with no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, I think, a good indication of good co-operation in the courtroom. Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir, no cross-examination, and therefore we don't see a reason for re-examination. No more questions for the witness. In that case, I can tell you, and you will be pleased, that this concludes your examination today. You are now free to return to your normal activities and to your home city. Thank you that you were able to come here to The Hague and to assist us. Thank you very much again, and the court usher will help you and assist you leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know Mr. Vanderpuye is following the proceedings. I don't know exactly right now where the next witness is, but he is obviously somewhere nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told he is already in the waiting room for the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Outstanding. Then I'm sure Mr. Vanderpuye will be here in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my business before the Trial Chamber. May I be excused for the rest of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, thank you very much for your attendance. Have a successful working day. Good morning, Mr. Vanderpuye. Welcome to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told the next witness is ready and waiting and should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before I forget, I think for this witness we are going to request a Rule 90 caution. He has maintained the status of a suspect since the very beginning, since his testimony, I think, in the Blagojevic case through the Popovic case. So I would ask that that instruction be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanic. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. You know you are here in the courtroom and you are obliged to tell the truth and nothing but the truth; however, on the request of the Prosecution, I would like to read out an article, Rule of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 90(E), and I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Witness, did you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye has some questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Once again, good morning. Good morning to you, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just before we get started, I just want to remind you to try to keep your voice up and to speak a little bit more slowly than you would normally so that the interpreters have a chance to translate what you say and what I say to all of the parties. If there's anything that I ask you that is unclear, please let me know. Now, what I'd like to ask you is do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor v. Vujadin Popovic et al. on 23 and 24 April 2007?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity prior to today to review the entirety of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes; yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you listen to the testimony on an audio recording?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having listened to your testimony in that case, do you stand by it? That is, does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I would like to tender Mr. Tanic's prior testimony. That will be P01177 and P01178, and I believe there are two associated exhibits with that testimony, which are P01129 (sic), and P01180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, which of the two exhibits with the transcript of the Popovic case are under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first, which is P01177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received under seal, and the other, 1178, will be received as well. I don't have a list of the exhibits here with me at the moment, therefore I would like to know whether these other two exhibits, 1129 and 1180, were used with this witness and tendered with the witness in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They were used with this witness and tendered through him, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I made a mistake. It's 1179. Let's clarify, Mr. Vanderpuye, on page 42, line 6, you were referring to P1129. Did you misspoke?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I did. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be P1179. Both exhibits will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks. I have a brief summary of Mr. Tanic's prior testimony, which I'd like to read into the record. Tanacko Tanic completed his military service with the JNA in 1981 and was be mobilized into the Territorial Defence in Zvornik, which in April 1992, became part of the Zvornik Brigade, where he served until his demobilisation in July 1996. In July 1995 Tanic was the treasurer in the finance section of the Brigade command. He was responsible for paying out soldiers' wages and dealing with payments and receipts concerning the requirements of the logistics unit. Tanic was responsible to the assistant commander for logistics, then Sreten Milosevic, as well as to the brigade commander, Vinko Pandurevic, to whom he often reported. On the morning of 14 July 1995, while on duty, Tanic saw a bus filled with Muslim prisoners outside the gates of the Standard Barracks compound. He later learned that the bus had previously travelled to various area schools to find a place to deposit the prisoners, but the prisoners spent the night on board. At around noon that day, Miladin Mijatovic approached Tanic, directed him to get his rifle, and told Tanic to come with him and a group of other Zvornik Brigade soldiers to Orahovac. According to Tanic, Mijatovic told him that the prisoners there were escaping. Tanic, who had already learned -- had already heard the prisoners were being detained in area schools, took up his rifle and, together with other soldiers, boarded a small truck outside the compound which took them to the Grbavci school in Orahovac. When they arrived, the soldiers disembarked near a fence surrounding the gym. Tanic could see members of the Zvornik Brigade military police and other soldiers already in the school-yard. It was readily apparent to Tanic that the prisoners had not in fact been escaping. For a time, Tanic stood on the road with Zvornik Brigade military policemen Cedo Jovic and Goran Bogdanovic, to prevent civilians from approaching the school-yard. At some point he entered the school-yard where he saw the dead bodies of two prisoners. He saw clothes piled up in front of the main entrance to the gym and there was even a crutch among them. Tanic saw Sreten Milosevic and assistant commander for security Drago Nikolic in the school-yard. He also saw an officer whom a military policeman identified to him as "a security officer from the corps, Vujadin Popovic." Tanic walked some distance away from the school building where he sat on the steps of a nearby cultural centre. From there he saw a young boy of 10 or 12 years of age accompanied by a VRS soldier walking along the rear of the school building toward the gym, carrying water. Although he had heard rumours about an exchange, and of Drago Nikolic's involvement in such negotiations, it became obvious to Tanic that the prisoners and the children were to be executed. Indeed, Tanic was asked directly by another soldier, "Come along, do you want to do some shooting?" Which he testified that he refused. Tanic remained near the school and gym for about two to three hours in all, until the first group of prisoners began boarding a small tarpaulin covered truck to carry them to the execution site. He then absented himself from the area and went to the home of a friend about a kilometre and a half away. He testified that he remained there until about 10.00 or 11.00 p.m. When he left, Tanic began walking along the roadside toward the Standard Barracks and could hear shooting in the distance. He was given a lift in a supply van that soon arrived. Inside were Mijatovic, Sreten Milosevic, Mihailo Stevanovic, and another person from the brigade's logistics unit, and a small boy from Srebrenica. If we can go into private session, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Although Tanic could not recall whether the van entered the compound upon arriving at Standard, he recalled that the soldiers nevertheless disembarked while the boy and the driver continued on to hospital. Tanic then returned to his office where he remained for some time. I have to go back into private session, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have concluded my summary and I have a few additional questions for the witness. If I could have, please, 65 ter 276 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, what I'm showing you hear is a 5th December, 1994, document. It's -- you can see it's issued here from the commander of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic. And what it is essentially is an appointment order. What I'd like to do is to take you to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Should be page 21 in B/C/S. First I think in the English we might have to go back one page just so we can see what is written there. Yes, that's great. We just need to go to the bottom of the page so we can match them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see at the bottom of the page there, Mr. Tanic, the heading "Financial Service." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under item number 35 there's a person there by the name of Drago Sakotic. Do you know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: He was head of the financial service in that period on the 5th of September, 1994 -- until the 5th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was his relation to you?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: He was my superior, my direct superior. I got assignments from him. He received them from the commander or the deputy commander for logistics, and I received assignments from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, let's turn -- we have to go to the next page in the English just for a moment. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And under Sakotic's name we can see there is the assignment as chief, and then is it says "until now" chief of the financial services and (b) "on records of the Zvornik MO." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To your recollection, was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was head of the service from July 1993. Head of the financial service. Before him, I was head of the service, and when he arrived in July 1993 he was appointed head and I was appointed treasurer of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, we can see that on this particular document under your name which is under item number 36. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And under your name, it says "as treasurer," that is, appointed as treasurer, and "until now, not assigned." And in 1995 was that the position that you occupied within the brigade, that is, position of treasurer of the financial service sector?

utterances.speaker: TANACKO TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
